name: Wei Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a firm that builds houses in a factory as big wall and floor panels, then we put them together on site like a giant flat-pack. I'm on the site crew, so when the lorry arrives at seven I'm guiding panels off the crane, lining them up, and fixing them down, and after that I'm on the inside finishing, doors, skirting, that kind of thing. A house goes up in four days, which still amazes me. I'm the new guy, and I'm slower with a nail gun than anyone, but I'm the one who reads the fixing schedules on my phone and spots when the factory's sent the wrong panel. The worst part is standing around when the crane's late and it's raining sideways.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-five years in IT support for a logistics company, fixing laptops and printers and resetting passwords. I got bored, and honestly I could see the chatbots doing most of my job before long. I'd sold some shares I'd held for years, the house is paid off, so at fifty-six I thought, why not learn something with my hands while I still can. My wife Lin does bookkeeping from home and she thought I'd lost my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it was overhyped, but the tools are still useful. I'd say that to the lads, and maybe post something about how I still use it every day for the boring bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest. I like this stuff, I use it every morning to check the fixing schedule and ask it why the engineer wants a certain bracket. If it stalls, I just carry on being slow with a nail gun and getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, practise my hand skills, and maybe ask the firm about a spot in the factory where they program the cutting machines. I'd keep my shares where they are. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A little flat, maybe, like a film that ends early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be disappointed. What were you hoping for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A site where the machine tells you exactly which panel goes where and checks your fixings with a camera, so we stop doing things twice. Last month we put up a whole gable end with the wrong window opening, and it took a day to fix. That's the kind of waste I'd love to see gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the others on the crew think of you checking things on your phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They teased me for about a month. Then I caught the wrong panel before it went up, saved us half a day, and now Darren, the crew leader, shouts across, Wei, ask your robot. I'll take that.

S0.say: I'd say it was overhyped but the tools are still useful. I'd tell the lads, and maybe post about how I still use it every day for the boring bits.
S0.think: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I like this stuff and use it every morning. If it stalls, I'll just keep getting better with a nail gun.
S0.do: Keeps working and practising his hand skills, and asks about a role in the factory programming the cutting machines. Leaves his shares where they are.
S0.feel: Fine but a little flat, like a film that ends early.
S0.quote: Then I caught the wrong panel before it went up, saved us half a day, and now Darren, the crew leader, shouts across, Wei, ask your robot.
S0.fieldNote: Wei is the only one on his crew who reads schedules on his phone, and he won the others over by catching a wrong panel. He'd be mildly disappointed if AI stalled, which is an unusual reaction for a construction worker. He left IT partly because he foresaw chatbots doing that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, and people should get ahead of it rather than complain. I don't think it's anybody's fault, it's just how things go. I'd say retrain early, it's cheaper than retraining late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. My firm is half factory already, so the change would hit the factory first, and I'm one of the few on site who'd actually enjoy running new kit. At fifty-eight, being the guy who understands the machines is the best job security I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a transfer to the factory, to work on the programs that cut the panels, within the year. I'd do an evening course on the cutting software, probably online, maybe a few hundred in fees. And I'd keep using the AI to check everything on site until they moved me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darren, honestly. He's brilliant with his hands but he won't touch a tablet. If the job turns into checking a screen as much as swinging a hammer, he'll hate it, and he's got two kids at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's nobody's fault. Would you say that to Darren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not in those words, no. I'd offer to show him the tablet stuff in the van at lunch. Saying it's nobody's fault doesn't pay his mortgage.

S1.say: I'd say it's a big change and people should get ahead of it instead of complaining. It's nobody's fault, and retraining early is cheaper than retraining late.
S1.think: Off the record, I think it's good for me. My firm is half factory already, and being the one who understands the machines is my best job security at fifty-eight.
S1.do: Asks for a transfer to the factory to program the panel-cutting machines within the year, and takes an online evening course in the cutting software for a few hundred. Keeps checking site work with AI meanwhile.
S1.quote: At fifty-eight, being the guy who understands the machines is the best job security I've got.
S1.fieldNote: Wei sees understanding the machines as his job security, not a threat. His 'nobody's fault' line softened when he thought about Darren, the crew leader who won't touch a tablet and has kids at school. He'd offer practical help in the van rather than speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan, quickly, and governments of any colour should sit down with the companies and sort out incomes for people. I'm not a big politics person, but two years is too fast for anybody to just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be all right. I've got the house, the savings, and I'd be sixty. But Lin's bookkeeping would be gone almost overnight, and my daughter Mia's in her second year studying accounting, which would be a wasted degree. That's what would keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd put some of our savings into the companies making the robots, because if they're taking the work, I'd rather own a slice. I'd talk to Mia about switching courses this year, not next. And I'd try to get a job keeping the site robots running, because they'll need someone who knows what a house is supposed to look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Interested, too, which feels odd to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why odd?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Lin would be losing her clients and I'd be sitting there reading about the robot specs with my tea. She'd catch me and say, you're enjoying this. And I'd have to admit, a little bit, yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mia about her course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm not going to tell her what to do, but she should look at the course list with fresh eyes. Something with people or machines in it, not spreadsheets. And I'd tell her we'll pay for the extra year if she switches.

S2.say: I'd say we need a plan quickly, with governments of any colour sitting down with companies to sort out incomes. Two years is too fast for anyone to shrug.
S2.think: Between us, I'd be all right with the house and savings at sixty. But my wife's bookkeeping would vanish and my daughter's accounting degree would be wasted, and that would keep me up.
S2.do: Invests some savings in robot-making companies and urges his daughter to switch courses this year, offering to pay for an extra year. Tries for a job keeping the site robots running.
S2.feel: Uneasy, and oddly interested, which he finds hard to admit.
S2.quote: She'd catch me and say, you're enjoying this. And I'd have to admit, a little bit, yes.
S2.fieldNote: His own job feels secondary; his wife's bookkeeping and his daughter's accounting degree are where the threat lands. He admits, with some guilt, that part of him finds the change exciting. His instinct is to own a slice of the companies doing the replacing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if you start now, and I'd tell people to start now. I'd probably bore everyone at the barbecue about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is perfect for me. I'd get my move into the factory, learn the machines properly, and be the experienced guy when the robots arrive on site at sixty-three. Lin would have time to move into something else, maybe advising small firms on the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the factory transfer this year and do the software course. In year two or three, I'd look for training on maintaining building robots, if anyone offers it. I'd put a slice of our savings into the robot companies over time, not all at once, and help Mia switch courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lin to do with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stop doing other people's books and start teaching them how to use the new tools, because she's patient and they trust her. She'd say she's too old for that. She said I was too old for building sites too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'a slice' of savings. How big a slice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a fifth of what we've got, spread over a few years. I don't know if it's a good bet, nobody does. But I'd rather be a bit wrong with a fifth than very wrong with all of it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if you start now, and I'd tell people to start now. I'd probably bore everyone at the barbecue about it.
S3.think: Honestly, five years is perfect: I'd move into the factory, learn the machines and be the experienced one when robots reach site at sixty-three. My wife would have time to change direction.
S3.do: Requests the factory transfer this year and does the software course, then seeks training in robot maintenance in years two or three. Puts about a fifth of savings into robot companies over a few years and helps his daughter switch courses.
S3.feel: Calm and honestly a bit excited.
S3.quote: I'd rather be a bit wrong with a fifth than very wrong with all of it.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Wei lays out a staged plan with numbers, including investing about a fifth of savings gradually. He admits nobody knows if it's a good bet. He pushes his wife to teach the new tools, echoing how others doubted his own late career change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so there's no reason for anyone to be caught out. I'd encourage the younger lads to pick up the tech side now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine either way. I'd be sixty-eight and probably retired, or doing a couple of days a week training people on the machines because I'd enjoy it. The robots might even make the last part of my working life easier on my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on site for a few years and get properly good with my hands, then move to the factory or a training role. I'd invest a bit at a time in the companies doing it. I'd use whatever new AI tools came along, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Looking forward to it, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darren, still, and the lads like him. Ten years is a long time if you start learning, and no time at all if you don't. I'd keep nagging him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your back. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After two years of lifting panels, my lower back tells me every morning I'm not thirty. If a robot holds the panel and I just guide it, I could do this till sixty-five. That would be a nice change.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time, so nobody should be caught out. I'd encourage the younger lads to pick up the tech side now.
S4.think: For me it's fine either way: I'd be sixty-eight, retired or training people part-time on the machines. Robots might even make my last working years easier on my back.
S4.do: Keeps working on site for a few years to improve his hand skills, then moves to the factory or a training role. Invests gradually in the companies building the robots and keeps using new AI tools.
S4.feel: Calm, and looking forward to it.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time if you start learning, and no time at all if you don't.
S4.fieldNote: Wei sees robots as a possible relief for his aching back that could extend his working life. His one lasting concern is Darren and workers who won't start learning. He treats ten years as plenty only for those who use it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, not for me, for Lin and Mia, because two years is no time to change direction. What would help is some kind of income for people while they retrain, and courses that actually exist before the jobs disappear, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd enjoy it. I would, parts of it. That's not a popular thing to say on a building site.

headlineQuote: I would, parts of it. That's not a popular thing to say on a building site.
portrait: Wei Schmidt is a 58-year-old new member of a site crew that assembles factory-built house panels, after 25 years in IT support that he left partly because he saw chatbots coming for it. With a paid-off house and savings from shares, he worries less about himself than about his wife Lin's bookkeeping and his daughter Mia's accounting degree. He uses AI every day, won his crew over by catching a wrong panel, and sees understanding the machines as his best job security. Across the scenarios he plans transfers, courses and gradual investments, and admits, a little sheepishly, that he'd enjoy parts of the change.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his wife and daughter would have no time to change direction.
whatWouldHelp: Income support for people while they retrain, and courses that exist before the jobs disappear, not after.
